The chart of captions sold as fact. Epstein is on it. The crimes were real. The client list, the murder finding, and the one-party scandal were not in the file.

This file holds 93 captions. Some are a cut tape or the wrong picture. Most are a word that was added, widened, or swapped until the sentence became a crime, a finding, or an order the recording does not contain. A few are the unequal standard in plain sight: one party’s scandal cut from logs that show both, one set of children used as a slogan while another count of children was treated as politics, a faith named when the order named countries, and one candidate called a danger so the law could be broken to stop him. A network is not a trustee under the United States Code. It asked the country to trust it with the record. An accurate report was the job it sold. These 93 lines are the breach of that job. The nation was divided along the caption. These 93 are the captions in this file. They are not every line that aired in twelve years.
What repetition does

Psychological warfare, on this page, is not a secret military program and it is not a basement plot. It is a method, and the method is ordinary. A short false sentence is easier to remember than a transcript. If a person hears that sentence every day, for months or for years, the mind stores it as something they saw. They will argue for it. They will not go find the tape, because the caption already feels like the tape.

The correction is long. The lie is six seconds, and it is repeated on the hour. That imbalance is the weapon. After enough repetitions, people defend the caption as if they watched the recording, and they sort a neighbor into an enemy without a statute. The length under each row is the point. That is how long the country was told to treat the caption as a fact.
Epstein

Epstein is on this chart because the crimes are real and the outrage was built past the file. He pleaded guilty in Florida in 2008. He was indicted again in New York in 2019. Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted and sentenced to twenty years. Those sentences are not a caption. What was manufactured is the rest. A client list the Justice Department and the FBI said the investigation did not find. A murder finding the medical examiner did not make. A one-party scandal cut from logs that show both worlds. The department’s July 2025 memorandum said there was no incriminating client list. The victims were then used as a slogan, while the children the government could not account for at the border were treated as a different argument. Both counts are children.
Why the slogan

The slogans were not descriptions. They were permission. Fine people. Bloodbath. Dictator. Bleach. Collusion. Threat to democracy. Clear and present danger. Each one was built to move an elected opponent out of politics and into the category of an extinction event. Once a man is an extinction event, the next sentence is always the same: ordinary law is too slow, so you may break it to stop him.

Clear and present danger is the cleanest case. Holmes wrote it in Schenck. Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 replaced it. The government may punish speech only if it is intended to produce imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. That sentence limits the state. It was used as the opposite of itself. Repeat the phrase until the public hears a finding. Then the FISA footnotes do not matter. The uncut tape is called context. A parody can stand in for the memo. A docket can be timed to an election and called accountability. 5 U.S.C. § 3331 is an oath to the Constitution, without any mental reservation. The charter has no clause that lets you break it to save it.

That is why the list below is long. A single lie can be corrected. A slogan, repeated, becomes the reason the next lie is allowed. The correction is not a favor to him. It is the minimum a republic owes the people who were told the law had been suspended.
Where the hours are

The Speaker’s release is not a speech. In November 2023 Speaker Johnson said the House would post 40,000 of about 44,000 hours and hold about 5 percent back for security. The Committee on House Administration’s Subcommittee on Oversight put the public Capitol Police CCTV on Rumble. The committee’s own notice of the releases is here. A public viewing room in the Capitol was what they offered while the website was still a fraction of the archive. The room was in Washington. The country was not. Calling a trip to the Capitol “public access” left the hours inaccessible to anyone who could not get there. On November 17, 2023, Speaker Johnson said the House would start posting video and that the room would let a citizen watch every minute uncensored in the meantime. He also said about 5 percent would stay back for security, and the online tapes were going to have faces blurred. The first post that day was about 90 hours, not 44,000. By March 22, 2024, the committee said almost 13,000 hours were online. On August 19, 2024, it posted another 6,000. A promise to release the tapes, followed by a room the country cannot travel to and a website that is still catching up, is not a release. The Epoch Times made two films, and a film is not the archive either. The Real Story of January 6 premiered July 22, 2022. The Real Story of January 6, Part 2: The Long Road Home followed in January 2024.
Said. Not invented.

These are not in the lie column, because he said them. “Fight like hell.” “Stand back and stand by.” “When the looting starts, the shooting starts.” The Access Hollywood tape, which he called “locker room talk. I’m not proud of it.” “I just want to find 11,780 votes.” The December 2022 post: a fraud that size “allows for the termination of all rules, regulations, and articles, even those found in the Constitution.” “Poisoning the blood.” “Vermin.” He told Bob Woodward on tape, March 19, 2020, “I wanted to always play it down.” A journal that hides those is doing the same work as the package that hides “peacefully and patriotically.”
The caption is not the recording. Read across.

The file: Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes are real. He pleaded guilty in Florida in 2008. He was charged again in the Southern District of New York in 2019. A July 2025 memorandum from the Justice Department and the FBI said the review found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence he blackmailed prominent people, and no basis to investigate uncharged third parties. The department said he harmed more than a thousand victims. A flight log is not that list. A contact book is not that list. The caption sold a document the investigation did not find.

How long it ran: From his death in August 2019, and louder in every campaign after it. The department’s memorandum is July 2025. The caption outlived the memorandum.

The file: The January 2017 assessment said Putin ordered an influence campaign and preferred him. It did not find that Donald Trump was an agent of Russia.

How long it ran: From the January 2017 assessment forward. The paper said Putin preferred him. “Agent” was added, and it ran for years.
Republicans paid Steele
They ran: Republicans funded the dossier. That is the whole story.
The file: The Clinton campaign and the DNC then paid Fusion GPS, which paid Steele. The FEC fined them for reporting that spending as legal services.
Record: fec.gov
How long it ran: From 2017. It buried the Clinton campaign and DNC payments. The FEC fine on that reporting came in 2022.
Don Jr. indicted
They ran: The Trump Tower meeting was the collusion, and Don Jr. was indicted.
The file: The June 9, 2016, meeting happened. No indictment of Donald Trump Jr. followed from it.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From the June 2016 meeting, told as an indictment through 2017–2019. He was not indicted.
Flynn the agent
They ran: Michael Flynn was convicted as a Russian agent under the Logan Act.
The file: He pleaded to a false statement. The Logan Act was not charged. The Justice Department moved to dismiss. A pardon followed. Agent and Logan Act were added.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From 2017 through the dismissal motion and the pardon in 2020. The Logan Act was never the charge.
Manafort colluded
They ran: Manafort was convicted of colluding with Russia.
The file: Paul Manafort was convicted of tax and bank-fraud counts. Collusion was not the conviction.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From the 2018 trial. Tax and bank fraud were the convictions. “Collusion” was glued on for years.
Stone and WikiLeaks
They ran: Roger Stone was convicted of conspiring with Russia.
The file: Stone was convicted of lying to Congress, obstruction, and witness tampering. A Russia-conspiracy count was not the verdict. A pardon followed.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From the 2019 verdict. Lying, obstruction, and witness tampering. The Russia-conspiracy caption was not the verdict.
Impeached for treason
They ran: They impeached him for treason.
The file: Treason is Article III and 18 U.S.C. § 2381. The first articles were abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. The second was incitement of insurrection. Treason was not the article.
Record: congress.gov
How long it ran: The 2019 impeachment and the 2021 impeachment. Treason was not the article either time.
Removed
They ran: He was impeached and removed.
The file: The House impeached him twice. The Senate acquitted him twice. Removal never happened.
Record: senate.gov
How long it ran: After both impeachments. The House impeached. The Senate did not remove him. The word “removed” still gets said.
The Senate convicted
They ran: The Senate convicted him of insurrection.
The file: The second trial ended 57–43. Conviction required two-thirds. He was acquitted.
Record: senate.gov
How long it ran: From the February 2021 vote, 57–43. Two-thirds was required. “Convicted” outlived the acquittal.
Already disqualified
They ran: The Fourteenth Amendment already knocked him off the ballot.
The file: Trump v. Anderson: states have no power to enforce Section 3 against a candidate for federal office. Congress holds that enforcement.
Record: supreme.justia.com
How long it ran: From the 2023 state cases until Trump v. Anderson on March 4, 2024. The ballot caption ran through a primary.
Hang Mike Pence
They ran: He told the crowd to hang Mike Pence.
The file: Rioters chanted “Hang Mike Pence.” At 2:24 p.m. he posted that Pence “didn’t have the courage.” The chant and the tweet are not the same words.
Record: govinfo.gov
How long it ran: From the afternoon of January 6. The crowd’s chant was assigned to his mouth, and it stayed assigned.
187 minutes
They ran: He watched television for 187 minutes and said nothing.
The file: He tweeted at 2:38 p.m. to stay peaceful and support the Capitol Police, and again at 3:13 p.m. to remain peaceful. The 4:17 p.m. video said go home. Silence is the altered word.
Record: c-span.org
How long it ran: From the 2022 hearings. “Said nothing” left out the 2:38 p.m. tweet, the 3:13 p.m. tweet, and the 4:17 p.m. video.
We love you
They ran: The video was only “we love you.”
The file: The same video told them to go home in peace. One clause was kept. The other was cut.
Record: govinfo.gov
How long it ran: From the January 6 video. One clause was kept. “Go home” was cut. That cut kept airing.
Never called the Guard
They ran: He never called the National Guard.
The file: The Defense Department’s timeline has a request and a deployment that afternoon. It was not instant. “Never” is the word that does not survive the timeline.
Record: documentcloud.org
How long it ran: From January 2021. The Defense Department timeline was public. “Never” outlasted it.
He grabbed the wheel
They ran: He grabbed the steering wheel and lunged at a Secret Service agent.
The file: That is hearing testimony. There is no video. Agents were reported ready to dispute it. Testimony is not a played tape.
Record: govinfo.gov
How long it ran: From the June 2022 hearing testimony. No video. It was reported as a played scene.
He quoted Hitler
They ran: He quoted Hitler on blood.

The file: On December 16, 2023, in Durham, New Hampshire, he said illegal immigrants are “poisoning the blood of our country.” That sentence is his. it is ugly. He did not read a line of Hitler on that tape. The phrase and a citation are not the same exhibit.
Record: c-span.org
How long it ran: From late 2023 into the 2024 campaign. The phrase is his. The claim of a direct quotation was added.
Five officers
They ran: Five police officers were killed by the mob that afternoon.
The file: Officer Sicknick died the next day of strokes, natural causes. Other deaths cited later were not killings on the Capitol steps that afternoon. The count was built by moving the clock.
Record: uscp.gov
How long it ran: From January 2021. The count was built by moving deaths onto that afternoon. It was repeated as a same-day toll.
Lost children
They ran: He lost 1,475 children.

The file: On April 26, 2018, HHS told a Senate subcommittee that caseworkers could not reach sponsors for 1,475 children on a follow-up call. The children had been released to sponsors. The agency said they were not lost. The number was printed as if it were family separation.
Record: hsgac.senate.gov
How long it ran: From the May 2018 follow-up number. Printed as children lost to family separation. The agency said they were not lost.
He invented separation
They ran: No child was separated before he invented it in 2018.

The file: Zero tolerance was announced April 6, 2018; DHS began referring all adult crossers for prosecution in May 2018. The HHS inspector general found that separations happened before that policy. The Flores settlement is 1997. “Invented” is the false word. The 2018 policy is real.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From zero tolerance in May 2018. “Invented” ignored the 1997 Flores settlement and earlier separations. It ran for years.
Concentration camps
They ran: The border facilities were concentration camps.
The file: The word is a specific historical crime. The places were CBP holding rooms. The word did the work the charge sheet did not.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From 2019. The historical word was applied to holding rooms and repeated through the border coverage.
Tear gas
They ran: They tear-gassed a peaceful crowd so he could hold a Bible.

The file: The inspector general found the clearing was for a fence, planned before the walk. Violence the two nights before had injured Park Police. The motive in the caption did not survive the report.
Record: doioig.gov
How long it ran: From June 1, 2020. The inspector general’s report is June 2021. The motive outlived the report.
He burned the church
They ran: He staged a photo at a church he had burned.
The file: St. John’s was damaged in a fire the night before the walk. He did not set it.
Record: doioig.gov
How long it ran: The week of June 1, 2020. The fire was the night before the walk.
Not one mile
They ran: He built nothing on the border.
The file: CBP records hundreds of miles of barrier in the first term, much of it replacement of older fence. Not zero. Not the full border he promised. “Nothing” is the lie.
Record: cbp.gov
How long it ran: Through the first term and the 2020 campaign. CBP’s mileage was public while “nothing” was the line.
Liable for rape
They ran: A jury found him liable for rape.
The file: In the Carroll case the verdict form was sexual abuse. The judge later said the conduct met a common meaning of rape. The form and the headline were not the same word.
Record: courtlistener.com
How long it ran: From the May 2023 verdict. The form said sexual abuse. The headline said rape, and the headline stuck.
Nuclear secrets
They ran: He was convicted of stealing nuclear secrets.
The file: The classified-documents indictment was dismissed. There was no conviction.
Record: storage.courtlistener.com
How long it ran: From the 2023 indictment through the 2024 dismissal. “Convicted” was said before any verdict, and there was no verdict.
Convicted of all of it
They ran: The 34 counts were insurrection, espionage, and rape.

The file: The Manhattan indictment is 34 counts of falsifying business records in the first degree, New York Penal Law § 175.10. A jury convicted on those counts. It is not a conviction for insurrection, espionage, or rape.
Record: manhattanda.org
How long it ran: From the May 30, 2024 verdict. Thirty-four false-record counts were stretched into insurrection, espionage, and rape.
Trump University
They ran: He was criminally convicted of fraud at Trump University.
The file: On November 18, 2016, the New York Attorney General announced a $25 million civil settlement. He did not admit the claim. There was no criminal conviction.
Record: web.archive.org
How long it ran: From the 2016 civil settlement. “Criminally convicted” was the added sentence, and it kept circulating.
The foundation
They ran: The Trump Foundation sent him to jail.
The file: On November 7, 2019, the New York Attorney General announced a court order dissolving the charity and a $2 million civil payment. He was not jailed.
Record: ag.ny.gov
How long it ran: From the 2019 civil dissolution. “Jail” was added. He was not jailed for it.
He pays no taxes
They ran: The leaked returns prove he pays no income tax. He is a cheat.

The file: Charles Littlejohn stole the returns while an IRS contractor, to influence the election. He pleaded guilty to unauthorized disclosure, 26 U.S.C. § 7213. He was sentenced to five years. The returns Ways and Means released in December 2022 show federal income tax paid: $641,931 in 2015, $750 in 2016, $750 in 2017, $999,466 in 2018, $133,445 in 2019, and $0 in 2020 on a reported loss. A low bill after losses and credits is not a charge that tax due went unpaid. No criminal tax-evasion case was brought on those returns. The man who went to jail is the man who leaked them.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From the 2020 leak through the December 2022 Ways and Means release, and after. Years of “pays nothing” against returns that show tax paid.
Most corrupt ever
They ran: He is the most corrupt president in American history.

The file: The caption ran for years. It was not a charge. His criminal conviction is 34 counts of falsifying business records in New York. It is not bribery, and it is not unpaid income tax. The comparison they would not run: House Oversight bank records show millions from foreign sources to Biden family members and associates. Hunter Biden sat on Burisma’s board while his father was vice president and the point man on Ukraine. A May 13, 2017 message on the laptop says “10 percent for the big guy.” Joe Biden said he never discussed the overseas business. The messages do not match that denial. Hunter was convicted on a gun count, pleaded guilty to tax counts, and was pardoned on December 1, 2024. Joe Biden was not convicted of bribery. One later FBI source who alleged a cash bribe was himself charged with lying. That charge does not erase the bank records or the board seat. Republicans opened an inquiry and did not make the country sit with this file the way the other side made the country sit with a caption.
How long it ran: From the first term through the later campaigns. Years. It was a caption. It was not a charge.
Suckers and losers
They ran: He called dead Marines suckers and losers. It is on tape.

The file: The Atlantic, September 3, 2020, used unnamed sources for a 2018 visit to a military cemetery. There is no recording. Trump denied it. Officials who were there denied it at the time. John Kelly later said he heard the words. A later recollection is not a tape. “On tape” is the added claim.
How long it ran: From The Atlantic, September 2020, through the election and after. There is still no recording.
Russian bounties
They ran: Russia paid the Taliban to kill American troops. It is confirmed.

The file: The New York Times printed it in June 2020. On April 15, 2021, the White House said U.S. intelligence assessed with low to moderate confidence that Russian intelligence officers sought to encourage Taliban attacks on U.S. and coalition personnel. Low-to-moderate confidence is not a confirmed order.
How long it ran: Summer 2020, printed as a certainty. Later assessments did not confirm it. The walk-back was quieter than the headline.
Liz Cheney
They ran: He called for Liz Cheney to be put in front of a firing squad.

The file: On October 31, 2024, in Glendale, he called her a radical war hawk and said to put her with a rifle, nine barrels shooting at her, so she would know what war is. That sentence is his, and it is ugly. It is a taunt about hawks and combat. It is not an order to execute a member of Congress.
How long it ran: The 2024 campaign. The firing-squad paraphrase traveled farther than the sentence.
Mostly peaceful
They ran: The protests were mostly peaceful.

The file: In the summer of 2020 a caption ran in front of fire. The Minneapolis Third Precinct burned. Kenosha burned. Insured losses from the unrest were about $1 billion to $2 billion. Peaceful assembly is a right. A police station on fire is not peaceful.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: The summer of 2020, including chyrons in front of fires. The season, and the clip after it.
Ban the pill
They ran: Day one, he will ban the abortion pill.
The file: He said he would not ban mifepristone. A caption is not a statute, and it is not his sentence.
Record: fda.gov
How long it ran: The 2024 campaign. He said he would not. The caption ran anyway.
Hands up
They ran: Hands up, don’t shoot. That is what happened.

The file: The Justice Department’s March 4, 2015 report on the shooting of Michael Brown found the credible evidence did not support that he had his hands up in surrender when he was shot. The slogan outlived the report.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From August 2014. The Justice Department report is March 4, 2015. The slogan outlived the report by years.
Rittenhouse
They ran: He crossed state lines with a rifle and murdered two Black men. A white supremacist.

The file: He lived in Illinois. The rifle was already in Wisconsin. The three people he shot were white. A jury acquitted him on November 19, 2021. “Crossed with the gun” and “killed Black people” were added. The verdict is the file.
How long it ran: From August 2020 through the November 19, 2021 acquittal, and after. The added words were not the case.
Horse paste
They ran: Ivermectin is horse paste. Only a fool would take it.

The file: On August 21, 2021 the FDA posted “You are not a horse.” Ivermectin is an FDA-approved drug for people. It was not approved for COVID-19. The caption erased the human drug and left the veterinary one. In 2024 the FDA settled a lawsuit and removed those posts. It did not change its view that the COVID trials had not shown a benefit.
Record: fda.gov
How long it ran: From the FDA post on August 21, 2021. Years as horse paste. The 2024 settlement removed the posts. It did not approve the drug for COVID.
Sharp as a tack
They ran: The president is sharp as a tack. The age talk is a smear.

The file: That caption ran until the June 27, 2024 debate. Special Counsel Robert Hur’s February 2024 report described “a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory.” The report was public for months while the caption said the opposite.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: From the Hur report in February 2024 until the debate on June 27, 2024. The report was public while the caption said the opposite.
Don’t say gay
They ran: Florida banned the word gay.
The file: The 2022 law limited classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in the early grades. It did not ban a word. The nickname replaced the statute.
How long it ran: From the 2022 Florida bill through the campaigns after it. The nickname replaced the text.
The noose
They ran: A noose was hung in Bubba Wallace’s garage to threaten him.

The file: On June 23, 2020, the U.S. Attorney and the FBI said no federal crime was committed. The rope had been in that garage since October 2019. Wallace was assigned the stall the week it was found. Nobody could have known he would get that stall. A hate crime was the first caption. The timeline did not support it.
Record: justice.gov
How long it ran: June 21 to 23, 2020. Two days as a hate crime. The FBI timeline was the next statement. The first caption traveled farther.
Zero inflation
They ran: Inflation is zero. Prices are down.

The file: In the summer of 2022 a month with little change was sold as inflation at zero. The yearly Consumer Price Index was still near 8 percent, after a 9.1 percent peak in June 2022. A flat month is not prices going back.
Record: bls.gov
How long it ran: Summer 2022. A flat month was sold as inflation over. The yearly index was still near 8 percent.
Vaccinated don’t carry
They ran: If you are vaccinated, you do not carry the virus and you cannot give it to anyone.

The file: That sentence was said in 2021, including by the CDC director on MSNBC on March 29, 2021. CDC data published July 30, 2021 showed vaccinated people could be infected and carry similar viral loads. A wish was reported as a finding.
Record: cdc.gov
How long it ran: From 2021. The sentence was treated as science. Later infections showed it was false when it was said.
She was in the chamber
They ran: She was in the Capitol chamber, in the mob, on January 6.

The file: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was in the Cannon House Office Building, which is connected by tunnel and was evacuated. She was not in the Senate or House chamber with the crowd that breached the Capitol. Fear can be real. The map in the caption was not.
How long it ran: From January 2021. The office building and the chamber were treated as the same room. The correction did not travel as far.
Kavanaugh
They ran: The accusation was corroborated. The hearing proved it.

The file: No witness at the September 2018 hearing corroborated the event as charged. The FBI’s supplemental background check did not produce a criminal charge. He was confirmed. Corroborated was the word the file did not earn.
Record: congress.gov
How long it ran: From the September 2018 hearing through the confirmation. “Corroborated” ran as if a witness had proved the event. No charge followed.
Smollett
They ran: A Trump-inspired hate crime. The attackers were his supporters.

The file: A jury later convicted him of disorderly conduct for filing a false report. On November 21, 2024 the Illinois Supreme Court overturned that conviction, because he had already taken a deal. The court did not find that the attack was real. The first caption used Trump’s name for a hoax.
Record: illinoiscourts.gov

How long it ran: January 2019, the week of the claim. A jury later convicted him of a false report. On November 21, 2024 the Illinois Supreme Court overturned that conviction because of an earlier deal. The court did not find the attack was real. The Trump-inspired version was the first telling.

entries.headline: How a dirty list goes to court.

lines: 90 days the notice a voter must send the state before suing over a dirty voter roll under the NVRA U.S. Code Open the record
52 U.S.C. § 20510 lets an aggrieved voter sue under the NVRA. U.S. Code
List maintenance is required by 52 U.S.C. § 20507. U.S. Code
A noncitizen voting in a federal election commits a crime (18 U.S.C. § 611). U.S. Code
The owner, in the owner’s words The tent does not need a palace. It needs a clean roll and a gavel. Clean the roll. Keep the gavel. Congress cannot be sued for being Congress.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
Congress cannot be sued for being Congress. A dirty voter list into court in 90 days. Step by step.

Congress cannot be sued for being Congress. The Speech or Debate Clause in Article I, Section 6 and the standing rule in Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife close that door. A dirty voter registration list into federal court. 52 U.S.C. § 20510 gives an aggrieved person a private right of action under the National Voter Registration Act. Written notice goes to the chief election official of the State. If the violation is not corrected in ninety days, the case may be filed in district court for an injunction. The court may award fees if the plaintiff prevails.
The tent does not need a palace. It needs a clean roll and a gavel. Clean the roll. Keep the gavel.

List maintenance is 52 U.S.C. § 20507. A noncitizen who votes in a federal election commits a crime under 18 U.S.C. § 611. Unlawful voting is a deportable offense under 8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(6). Names go to the United States Attorney. The United States Attorney files. That is the lawful path. It is slow. It is real.

Bringing in and harboring certain aliens is 8 U.S.C. § 1324. Records of federal grants sit under the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552. A class action that claims to vacate the House will be dismissed. Powell v. McCormack and Luther v. Borden already said why. Anyone selling that suit is selling a dismissal.
The next essay is who to call, with addresses, not a stranger on a video asking for the card.

lines: 90 days notice to the state's chief election official comes first, not a class action against the House U.S. Code Open the record
The first step is a 90-day NVRA notice to the state election chief. U.S. Code
Groups that already file voter-roll cases publish their own dockets. judicialwatch.org
Names of noncitizens who voted go to the U.S. Attorney (18 U.S.C. § 611). U.S. Code
The owner, in the owner’s words The groups that already sue are the path. A clip is not a lawsuit. Real groups. Real addresses. Not a stranger on a video asking for money.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
Real groups. Real addresses. Not a stranger on a video asking for money.

This journal is not a law firm. The first envelope is a ninety-day notice under 52 U.S.C. § 20510, sent to the chief election official of the State, not a class action against the House. A check mailed to a stranger on a video has left the docket.
The groups that already sue are the path. A clip is not a lawsuit.

For dirty voter rolls, start with counsel that already files National Voter Registration Act cases: Judicial Watch, America First Legal, and the Public Interest Legal Foundation. Those are their own sites. This journal does not vouch for a donation. It names who already knows how to write the ninety-day letter.

For sanctuary ordinances and public-benefit spending past 8 U.S.C. § 1621, the Immigration Reform Law Institute and FAIR publish their own dockets. A state attorney general and the United States Attorney for the district are the public offices. Names of noncitizens who voted in a federal race go to the United States Attorney under 18 U.S.C. § 611.
The envelope is a name, the statute, the records, and no manifesto.

entries.headline: They're spending taxpayer money on illegal immigrants.

sources.label: Justice Department record Open the record

lines: “is not eligible for any Federal public benefit” 8 U.S.C. § 1611(a), on an alien who is not a qualified alien (narrow exceptions apply) U.S. Code Open the record
Federal law bars most federal benefits for aliens who are not qualified. U.S. Code
States need their own post-1996 law to give state benefits (8 U.S.C. § 1621). U.S. Code
DOJ has sued jurisdictions that give illegal aliens in-state tuition. Justice Department record
The owner, in the owner’s words Article VI is the same article as the oath. They swore it. Then they spent past it with taxpayer money.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
Federal law already limits public benefits for illegal immigrants. Governors still paid for hotels, debit cards, and clothes.

Federal law already said who may receive a public benefit. 8 U.S.C. § 1611 makes an alien who is not a qualified alien ineligible for federal public benefits, with narrow exceptions such as emergency medical care and short-term shelter or other aid the Attorney General deems necessary to protect life or safety. 8 U.S.C. § 1621 does the same for state and local public benefits unless a state enacted an affirmative law after August 22, 1996. In-state tuition has its own bar in 8 U.S.C. § 1623. Our view: a prepaid card, a clothing stipend, and months in a hotel are not an emergency room, and a governor who spends them on people the statute bars, without the state law the statute requires, is spending past supreme federal law.
Article VI is the same article as the oath. They swore it. Then they spent past it with taxpayer money.

Article VI makes the Constitution and federal statutes the supreme law of the land. Arizona v. United States held that federal law occupies the field of alien registration and preempted three of the four Arizona provisions at issue. A state need not loan its police to ICE. A state may not run a welcome mat federal law closed. 8 U.S.C. § 1373 forbids a gag on exchanging immigration-status information with federal officials. 8 U.S.C. § 1324 is harboring. That is a United States Attorney case, not a kitchen-table complaint against a sitting governor.

The Department of Justice has filed complaints against jurisdictions that give illegal aliens in-state tuition. HHS restored the 1996 welfare restrictions on its own programs. Those dockets are the file. The statute does not supply a prison date. The ordinance and the contract go to the United States Attorney, who decides whether harboring is in the record.
The next lever is the legislature that can repeal the post-1996 statute, and the voter who hires that legislature.

lines: “shall take into custody” 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c), on certain criminal aliens U.S. Code Open the record
Federal law directs detention when no release condition protects the public. U.S. Code
The Attorney General “shall take into custody” certain criminal aliens. U.S. Code
Minnesota's U.S. Attorney won a 28-year sentence in the Feeding Our Future fraud. U.S. Attorney record

The owner, in the owner’s words The statute said shall. The robe said walk. The public paid. This is why the street feels like a siege. Oversight is a docket, a retention vote, and a legislature that can repeal cashless-bail experiments that the blood already tested.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
When a court sends a dangerous defendant home, the statute already said otherwise. This is why the street feels like a siege.

Federal detention law is not a suggestion. 18 U.S.C. § 3142 directs a court to detain a defendant when no condition of release will reasonably assure the safety of any other person and the community. 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c) says the Attorney General shall take into custody certain criminal aliens. When a court or a local statute sends a repeat felon home on an ankle monitor, the statute said shall and the robe said walk.
The statute said shall. The robe said walk. The public paid.

This journal will not recycle a local news item as if it were a federal finding. Name the charging document. Name the statute. If a judge released a defendant who then killed a police officer, the remedy is the record, the appellate court, impeachment or failure to retain under Article I and Article II where those tools apply, and the next election of the district attorney and the bench the state elects. It is not a crowd at the courthouse door.

The United States Attorney for the District of Minnesota obtained a twenty-eight-year sentence in the Feeding Our Future fraud. That is a federal judgment. State sentencing grids are a different file. They stay on separate ledgers.
Oversight is a docket, a retention vote, and a legislature that can repeal cashless-bail experiments that the blood already tested.

sources.label: Supreme Court opinion Open the record

lines: “They work for us. They do not get to grade their own homework.” The owner, in the owner’s words
U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton (1995): states cannot term-limit Congress. Supreme Court opinion
Article V: how the Constitution is amended. U.S. Constitution
The STOCK Act of 2012. Public law

The owner, in the owner’s words What the amendment should do, in plain words. One: every seat turns over on a clock — House and Senate — no career. Two: they do not set their own pay, stock rules, or ethics. Those go to a citizen oversight board.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
Replace them. Term-limit them. They do not get to write their own privileges. A citizen board that also goes home.

A suspect does not write the criminal code. Congress writes its pay, its pension, its ethics office, and the exceptions that keep the political club comfortable. Then it investigates itself. That is not oversight. That is a club with a gavel. The people who work for us have become a class that cannot be fired except in theory, every two or six years, by a map they drew and a pile of money they raised from the lobby named above.

Term limits cannot be passed as a regular bill. The Supreme Court said so in 1995 — U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton. States may not add extra qualifications to get into Congress. So it takes an amendment. Article V: two-thirds of both houses, or two-thirds of the states call a convention; three-fourths of the states must say yes. There is no other lawful door. There is no extra-constitutional door. This journal does not preach one.

What the amendment should do, in plain words. One: every seat turns over on a clock — House and Senate — no career. Two: they do not set their own pay, stock rules, or ethics. Those go to a citizen oversight board. The board is term-limited too. No one on it may run for Congress later. If the watchers can become the watched, that is another club. Three: the laws they pass bind them. No special healthcare, no special exemptions, no insider trades dressed as ‘timing.’ The STOCK Act of 2012 was a press conference. The trades continued.
They work for us. They do not get to grade their own homework.

Why replace this Congress, not tutor it: the people who would have to vote away their own privileges will not. That is the whole problem in one sentence. So the states must. Later lessons: the text of a draft amendment, how an Article V call works, and why a citizen board that never goes home would become the next swamp. The overseers go home too. Or it is nothing.

Assaulting a federal officer is a crime (18 U.S.C. § 111). U.S. Code
Publishing an officer's home address to enable threats is a crime (18 U.S.C. § 119). U.S. Code
June 23, 2026: eight people sentenced in the Prairieland attack (DOJ). Justice Department record
The owner, in the owner’s words How it ends. Charge the person who did the act. Prairieland is the example.
more: The verified text, checked against primary records on Sep 24, 2026. Passages marked are opinion.
Assault, a published address, and a threat to a juror are already crimes. The funding file does not name a donor. The charge sheet names the people who did the act.

Peaceable assembly is a right. The First Amendment says so. A bottle, a published home address, a vehicle used as a weapon, and a threat to a juror are not assembly. They are already crimes. Ending them is a charge, not a second mob.

DHS, January 8, 2026: from January 20 through December 31, 2025, the department recorded 275 assaults on ICE officers, against 19 in the same stretch of 2024. Vehicular attacks in a nearly identical window: 66, against 2. The department’s line for doxxing and harassment of those officers is 866-347-2423.

The statutes do not need a new slogan. 18 U.S.C. § 111 is assault on a federal officer. 18 U.S.C. § 119 is publishing a covered person’s home address so that another person can threaten or harm him. 18 U.S.C. § 1361 is government property. 18 U.S.C. § 1503 is influencing, intimidating, or impeding a juror. The ordinary maximum is 10 years. If the trial is a criminal case, the juror is a petit juror, and a class A or B felony was charged, the maximum is 20 years.

Prairieland is what the charge looks like when it is brought. On July 4, 2025, an attack at the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas wounded a local police officer. The Justice Department, June 23, 2026: eight people sentenced for rioting, weapons, explosives, material support to terrorists, obstruction, and the attempted murder. Benjamin Hanil Song, convicted of the attempted murder, received 100 years. The eight sentences together were 450 years. The department called them an Antifa cell, and called the case the first such sentencing after a September 2025 executive order that designated the movement a domestic terrorist organization. The label is the government’s. The years are for the attack. An idea does not carry a rifle. A person does.

A juror is not a target, from either side. Section 1503 does not ask which party is angry. This journal will not assign juror threats to a party without the charging document. In People v. Trump the court kept jurors’ identities from the public because it found a risk of harassment. “They dox jurors” as a party caption, with no charge sheet, is the same alteration this journal refuses everywhere else.

Who paid for it. The Prairieland release does not name a donor who bought the weapons. 26 U.S.C. § 6104 keeps most contributor names off the public Form 990. Congress appropriates. An agency writes a grant. A nonprofit cashes it. The country often cannot see the name on the check. That darkness is not proof that a named person purchased the attack. It is proof the ledger is closed. A rumor treated as a conviction is a caption.

How it ends. Charge the person who did the act. Prairieland is the example. Use the statutes already in the code: § 111, § 119, § 1361, and § 1503. Report an officer’s published address to the department, not to a crowd. Congress holds the purse under Article I, Section 9. A grant with no public itemized ledger is a door. Close the grant, or open the ledger. The form does not name the donor. The donor is not invented. Then the ballot. A member who tells the country that the enforcement agency is the enemy, while assaults on its officers rise from 19 to 275 in a year, is not doing the oath in 5 U.S.C. § 3331. The answer to a mob is not a second mob.

lines: August 2020: Democrats told the country the Postal Service was being dismantled so a ballot would die in a bin. November 12, 2020: CISA called the contest ‘the most secure in American history.’
The ‘most secure’ sentence was about voting systems: paper backups so a hacked tally can be checked. That is a claim about machines, not the mail.
CISA did not audit the kitchen. It issued a press release about the tabulator.
The Intelligent Mail barcode is a routing mark so a sorter knows which bin. Tracking is not identity.
August 2026: USPS finalized a rule with a federal portal and two unique barcodes per mail voter.
more: The same USPS they called sabotaged in August they called the courier of the most secure election in history in November. The extra security they now advertise is a sorting sticker. Make it make sense.
The Intelligent Mail barcode — IMb — is sixty-five bars the Postal Service prints so a sorter knows which bin.
It is the same family of mark that rides on a catalog and a utility bill.
BallotTrax and the county software can ping when the envelope is scanned.
Tracking is not identity.
The envelope is supposed to carry a signature.
Signatures are matched by a clerk under rules that vary by state, by county, by how tired the clerk is at 9 p.m.
The barcode does not watch the kitchen table.
It does not watch who filled the oval.
It does not watch who licked the flap.
It watches a piece of paper go through a camera in a plant.

People voted by mail for decades before 2020 — mostly absentee, mostly with an excuse, mostly in numbers the plants could swallow. 2020 made the exception the system and then forbade asking how a letter becomes a vote.
The honest design is in-person, with identification, or absentee with a reason and a chain a court can read.
A sorting sticker on a pandemic envelope is not that.
It is a caption that says ‘trust us’ in machine-readable ink.
Let them hear us now — including the summer they said the mail was dying and the November they said it had never been safer.

lines: The method is a sentence cut just short of the Supreme Court’s incitement test: they do not say ‘torch the precinct.’ They say create a crowd.
June 23, 2018, Maxine Waters: “you get out and you create a crowd and you push back on them.” February 9, 2020, Ayanna Pressley: “we will bring the fire.”
June 1, 2020, Kamala Harris urged donors to a bail fund for protesters in Minnesota. July 9, 2020, Nancy Pelosi on a toppled statue: “People will do what they do.”
The unrest of May 26 to June 8, 2020 was classified a catastrophe across more than twenty states; the Insurance Information Institute put insured losses at one to two billion dollars.
The Member keeps clean hands. The city pays.
more: Careful words. A crowd takes the hint. Cities burn. Insurers counted a billion. The Member still has the chair.
So they do not say “torch the precinct at eight.” They say create a crowd.
They should not let up.
People will do what they do.
The crowd hears the rest.
The Member keeps clean hands.
A parking lot already knows what a crowd is for.

On February 9, 2020, Representative Ayanna Pressley, with the Squad, said: “If you don’t see the light, then we will bring the fire.” RealClearPolitics has the tape. Fire is a metaphor until it is not.
She named a method.
She said they should not let up.
On July 9, 2020, Speaker Nancy Pelosi was asked about a Columbus statue pulled down and thrown in Baltimore’s harbor.
She said, “People will do what they do.” That is the cleanest pair of hands in the record: a shrug from the Speaker while property comes down.
On December 8, 2020, Michigan State Representative Cynthia Johnson of Detroit posted: “This is just a warning to you Trumpers.
We ain’t playing with you. … And for those of you who are soldiers, you know how to do it.
Make them pay.” AP · MLive .
She had been threatened with lynching.
The next day she said “soldiers” meant soldiers of Christ.
The first tape still says “you know how to do it.” The House stripped her committees.
No prosecutor took that incitement test into court.

Property Claim Services, a Verisk unit that has tracked insured civil-disorder losses in this country since 1950, classified the unrest of May 26 through June 8, 2020, as a catastrophe — the first time it had to treat a civil-disorder event as multi-state, across more than twenty states.
The Insurance Information Institute put the insured range at one to two billion dollars.
That beat the prior record, the 1992 Los Angeles riots, which PCS had at $775 million.
They are the part an actuary would sign.
Small shops that had no policy, or a deductible that ate the rebuild, are not in that number.
City overtime is not in that number.
National Guard pay is not in that number.
Those land on the taxpayer and on the premium the rest of us pay the next year.
The people who said create a crowd, bring the fire, they should not let up, people will do what they do, did not receive an invoice.
They kept the chair.
The incitement test covers the rally and the talk show if no prosecutor can prove imminence.
The arsonist, if caught, is a local case.
The Member is a national brand.
That is the split: rage is delegated.
A march that stays on the sidewalk is the right.
On the night of May 28, 2020, the Minneapolis Third Precinct was abandoned and burned.
It is a municipal building used by the people who are paid to keep a city.
The next weeks, other cities copied the method.
The partners in the newsroom supplied the caption.
CNN put a Kenosha fire on the screen and a caption under it: “fiery but mostly peaceful protests.” The fire was not a graphic.
That is gaslight: a word for when an institution asks a country to distrust the evidence of the senses so the speaker can keep clean hands.
“Mostly peaceful” is how the arson is hidden inside the assembly.
If ninety-nine people walk and one person lights the precinct, the honest sentence is that a precinct burned.
The dishonest sentence is that the night was mostly a march.
The Member who said they should not let up, and the anchor who said it was mostly peaceful, are doing the same job from two desks.
One heats the crowd.
One launders the heat.
The taxpayer still pays for the building.

What was done to that station, and to storefronts across twenty states, was not peaceable, was not assembly, and was not covered as crime by the people whose job is to describe what is in front of the camera.

more: Medicare for All is not a slogan. It is $32–34 trillion in extra federal spending in ten years — more than a full year of everything America produces — on a Treasury that already cannot close a $1.9 trillion hole.
With arithmetic that is already in motion.
CBO has net interest doubling in a decade under current law — before Medicare for All.
Add $3 trillion-plus a year in new federal outlays and the Treasury is not ‘covering health care.’ It is bidding against every mortgage, every factory, every payroll in the market for dollars.
It is how a reserve currency becomes a warning label.
Hospitals that cannot hire because the reimbursement is a political number.
Drugs that do not get made because the price is a press conference.
A generation that inherits a 120-percent-of-GDP debt plus a new entitlement that cannot be unwound without a riot in the caption.

lines: The advocates’ own number is $10 trillion to $16 trillion (Darity: $10–12 trillion at Brookings, 2020; $16 trillion ‘the floor,’ 2026).
H.R. 40 has been introduced since 1989. It does not pay anyone. It studies. Ninety-six cosponsors in 2025.

more: Reparations returns every election because it is a loyalty test that never has to clear a bank. The advocates’ own number is $10–16 trillion. The Treasury does not have it. The Constitution does not permit a race-line from the IRS.
Because it is cheap as politics and impossible as math.
In a Democratic primary it is a loyalty test: say the word or be called a denier of history.
In a general election it is quietly dropped, because the country is not 13 percent of the electorate and does not write blank checks by race.
Washington State Democrats put ‘implementation’ into a platform in June 2026 — after Juneteenth, on a weekend, in a room of delegates.
Not the Budget Committee.
The weekend the cameras want a moral.
California proved the rest.
Gavin Newsom signed a task force, took the applause, and when the economists put $1.2 million per person on the table he would not write it.
The 2024 budget set aside $12 million for ‘reparations legislation.’ Twelve million is a press release.
The pattern is the product: commission, headline, no check.
A study cannot be opposed without the charge of opposing history.
That is why they prefer H.R. 40 to a scored bill.
A study has no Joint Committee on Taxation table.
A study cannot be defeated on arithmetic.
A study can be reintroduced forever.
This journal will not deny slavery, Jim Crow, or redlining.
The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments were the legal end of the slave power.
The Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act were the legal end of Jim Crow.
A country can teach that without lighting a race line under the income tax.
What it cannot do is add a $16 trillion racial outlay on top of a $34 trillion health outlay and call the sum justice.
That is how the currency is destroyed, the courts, and the idea that the law is the same for the man in the next pew.
The Hearing’s demand is the same as it was for Medicare for All.
Name the pay-for.
Name the eligible class without a racial test that dies in court.
No pay-for, no slogan.
Let them hear us now — including the part where the check never existed.

entries.headline: What the autopsy and toxicology found

lines: Other significant conditions: "Arteriosclerotic and hypertensive heart disease; fentanyl intoxication; recent methamphetamine use." HCME
Severe multifocal arteriosclerotic heart disease; enlarged heart (540 g). "No life-threatening injuries identified"; no injury to the neck structures or larynx. Autopsy
Hospital blood: fentanyl 11 ng/mL; methamphetamine 19 ng/mL. Autopsy, toxicology

Prosecutor's memo of a May 31 call: Dr. Baker called the fentanyl level "pretty high"; the memo summarizes it as "a fatal level of fentanyl under normal circumstances" and records that he would have concluded overdose if Floyd had been found dead at home with no other contributing factors. Exhibit 4, State v. Thao
Cause: "Cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression." Manner: "Homicide." HCME
Armed Forces Medical Examiner: "agrees with the autopsy findings and the cause of death certification"; "We concur with the reported manner of death of homicide." AFME consult
Chauvin: jury convicted on all three counts (Apr 20, 2021); 270 months; affirmed on appeal; U.S. Supreme Court denied review (Nov 20, 2023). Minn. Ct. App. Docket 23-416

Federal plea: Chauvin admitted his force "impaired Mr. Floyd's ability to obtain and maintain sufficient oxygen to sustain Mr. Floyd's life." Plea agreement Thao, Kueng and Lane were convicted federally. Thao verdict

entries.headline: 1.1 The Hennepin County Medical Examiner's findings

lines: On June 1, 2020, the Hennepin County Medical Examiner's Office gave the cause of death as "Cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression." (HCME press release, June 1, 2020)
The same release listed the manner of death as "Homicide." (HCME press release)
Under "How injury occurred" it stated: "Decedent experienced a cardiopulmonary arrest while being restrained by law enforcement officer(s)." (HCME press release)
Under "Other significant conditions" it listed: "Arteriosclerotic and hypertensive heart disease; fentanyl intoxication; recent methamphetamine use." (HCME press release)
more: The release also stated: "Manner of death is not a legal determination of culpability or intent, and should not be used to usurp the judicial process." (HCME press release)
The full autopsy report was signed by Dr. Andrew M. Baker on June 1, 2020. It records the death as occurring on May 25, 2020 at 9:25 p.m. (Autopsy report 2020-3700, archived county copy)
The autopsy lists "Arteriosclerotic heart disease, multifocal, severe," along with hypertensive heart disease and an enlarged heart weighing 540 grams. (Autopsy report)
It records "No life-threatening injuries identified" and notes no petechiae and no injury to the neck structures or larynx. (Autopsy report)

The autopsy found sickle cell trait (hemoglobin S 38%), with no sickling before death. It also recorded a positive test for SARS-CoV-2 RNA, which the report judged "most likely" to be leftover positivity from Floyd's known infection in April 2020. (Autopsy report)
Toxicology on hospital blood drawn before death (NMS Labs) reported the following (Autopsy report, toxicology section):
fentanyl 11 ng/mL
norfentanyl 5.6 ng/mL
4-ANPP 0.65 ng/mL
methamphetamine 19 ng/mL
delta-9 THC 2.9 ng/mL
11-hydroxy delta-9 THC 1.2 ng/mL
delta-9 carboxy THC 42 ng/mL
urine morphine (free) 86 ng/mL
The lab's reference notes in the report state: "In fatalities from fentanyl, blood concentrations are variable and have been reported as low as 3 ng/mL." (Autopsy report)
The same notes state: "Blood levels of 200 - 600 ng/mL have been reported in methamphetamine abusers who exhibited violent and irrational behavior." (Autopsy report)

entries.headline: 1.2 What the medical examiner told prosecutors before the final report (court exhibits)

lines: A Hennepin County Attorney's Office memo dated May 26, 2020, filed as an exhibit in State v. Thao, records that "[t]he autopsy revealed no physical evidence suggesting that Mr. Floyd died of asphyxiation." It also notes that the final report was not yet complete. (Exhibit 3, State v. Thao, 27-CR-20-12949)

A June 1, 2020 prosecutor's memo in the same filing summarizes a May 31, 2020 call with Dr. Baker about the final toxicology results. It records that Dr. Baker called the fentanyl level of 11 "pretty high," and that he described methamphetamine at 19 ng/mL as "very near the low end" and "a stimulant hard on the heart." (Exhibit 4, State v. Thao)

The memo's summary, written in the memo author's own words, continues: "This level of fentanyl can cause pulmonary edema. Mr. Floyd's lungs were 2-3x their normal weight at autopsy. That is a fatal level of fentanyl under normal circumstances." (Exhibit 4, State v. Thao)

The memo also records, in paraphrase: "AB said that if Mr. Floyd had been found dead in his home (or anywhere else) and there were no other contributing factors he would conclude that it was an overdose death." (Exhibit 4, State v. Thao)

The medical examiner's final certification, issued the same day, listed fentanyl as an "other significant condition" and not as the cause of death. The certified cause and manner were those stated above. (HCME press release)

At the request of the U.S. Department of Justice, the Office of the Armed Forces Medical Examiner reviewed the case (DoD Case Consult C0022-20, dated June 10, 2020). Its report was later filed as Exhibit 5 in State v. Thao. (AFME consult, Exhibit 5)

The AFME wrote: "The Office of the Armed Forces Medical Examiner agrees with the autopsy findings and the cause of death certification of George Floyd as determined by the Hennepin County Medical Examiner's Office." (AFME consult)

It continued: "His death was caused by the police subdual and restraint in the setting of severe hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and methamphetamine and fentanyl intoxication. The subdual and restraint had elements of positional and mechanical asphyxiation. The presence of sickle cell trait is a significant finding in this context." (AFME consult)
It concluded: "We concur with the reported manner of death of homicide." (AFME consult)

The trial-testimony summaries below come from Judge Peter Cahill's written Verdict, Findings of Fact, and Conclusions of Law in State v. Thao (filed May 1, 2023). That document cites the Chauvin trial transcript by page. (Thao verdict)
Hennepin County Medical Examiner Dr. Andrew Baker (called by the State)

Dr. Baker testified that "the law enforcement subdual restraint and the neck compression was just more than Mr. Floyd could take by virtue of those heart conditions" (Chauvin Tr. 4889–4890). (Thao verdict)
He testified that fentanyl and methamphetamine contributed to the death but were not "the direct cause" (Chauvin Tr. 4890–4911). (Thao verdict)
more: He agreed that "[h]ad Mr. Floyd been home alone in his locked residence with no evidence of trauma, and the only autopsy finding was that fentanyl level" he "would certify his death as due to fentanyl toxicity" (Chauvin Tr. 4932). (Thao verdict, n.60)
He testified that carbon monoxide "played no role in [Floyd's] death" (Fed. Tr. 1426–1427). (Thao verdict)
The court wrote: "The Court finds Dr. Baker's testimony credible." (Thao verdict)
Defense expert Dr. David Fowler (forensic pathologist; formerly Chief Medical Examiner for the State of Maryland, per the court's findings)

Dr. Fowler testified that the death was caused by "[c]ardiac arrhythmia due to hypertensive atherosclerotic disease during restraint" (Chauvin Tr. 5505). He also testified that Floyd did not die of asphyxia (Chauvin Tr. 5522). (Thao verdict)
He testified that several other factors contributed (Chauvin Tr. 5475): possible carbon monoxide from the squad-car exhaust, methamphetamine, fentanyl, and a paraganglioma (a tumor). (Thao verdict)
He testified that Chauvin's knee was "nowhere close to [Floyd's] airway" (Chauvin Tr. 5542). (Thao verdict)
On cross-examination he made four concessions (Thao verdict): He had not seen any laboratory results for Floyd's carbon monoxide levels (Chauvin Tr. 5565–5568).
There was "only a very low level of methamphetamine" (Chauvin Tr. 5497, 5617).
Floyd did not show the "outward symptoms" of a fentanyl overdose (Chauvin Tr. 5614).
Floyd "should have been given immediate emergency attention" when he went into cardiac arrest (Chauvin Tr. 5604).

The court wrote: "The Court finds Dr. Fowler's ultimate conclusions and opinions unpersuasive." It noted that he "lacks expertise and clinical experience in pulmonology, cardiology, and toxicology." (Thao verdict)
Other prosecution experts

Forensic pathologist Dr. Lindsey Thomas testified that asphyxia was the primary mechanism of death and agreed with the homicide certification. She also testified that Floyd would not have died on May 25, 2020 "except for the interactions with law enforcement" (Chauvin Tr. 4753, 4778–4779, 4793–4794). (Thao verdict)
NMS Labs toxicologist Dr. Daniel Isenschmid testified to three points (Chauvin Tr. 4610–4633). The court found his testimony credible. (Thao verdict)
The methamphetamine level of 19 ng/mL was "very low."
That level was in the "bottom 5.9 percent" of 3,271 DUI cases.
The median in those DUI cases was 240 ng/mL.
In the federal trial, Dr. Vikhyat Bebarta, described by the court as "a board-certified emergency physician and medical toxicologist," testified to three points (Fed. Tr. 2128). (Thao verdict)
Floyd's 11 ng/mL fentanyl level "was also low."
Doctors typically give 11 to 20 ng/mL to patients during complex procedures.
Patients who die from fentanyl overdoses "typically have levels of 40 ng/mL or higher."
Pulmonologist Dr. Martin Tobin testified that Floyd's oxygen level had fallen to zero by 8:25:41 p.m. The court found this testimony credible (Tobin, Tr. 4531–4532). (Thao verdict)
How the parties characterized the evidence on appeal

Chauvin's appellate brief, which is a party's argument and not a finding, stated that Dr. Baker testified to no physical evidence of asphyxia. It also described the fentanyl level as "three times the amount considered fatal." (Appellant's brief, A21-1228)
The State's brief, also a party's argument, described Dr. Fowler's opinion as arrhythmia with "significant contributory conditions" (T. 5475). (Respondent's brief, A21-1228)

lines: In the Chauvin trial, the defense called MPD Officer Scott Creighton and paramedic Michelle Moseng to testify about a prior encounter with Floyd on May 6, 2019. (Thao verdict, n.32)

Judge Cahill found both witnesses credible. He wrote that "although Floyd displayed some initial indications of noncompliance in the May 6, 2019 incident … none of the officers involved during that incident found it necessary to engage in use of force." (Thao verdict, n.32)
Chauvin's appellate brief argued that the trial court limited evidence from the 2019 incident. (Appellant's brief)

entries.headline: 1.6 Derek Chauvin: state conviction and appeals

sources.label: Order reproduced in cert. petition appendix, No. 23-416

lines: Testimony in State v. Chauvin ran from March 29 to April 15, 2021. The jury returned guilty verdicts on all three charges on April 20, 2021. (Thao verdict, procedural history)
The three charges were second-degree unintentional murder, third-degree murder, and second-degree manslaughter. (Minn. Ct. App. opinion A21-1228)
On June 25, 2021, the court entered a conviction for second-degree unintentional murder and imposed 270 months. (Thao verdict)
The Minnesota Court of Appeals affirmed on April 17, 2023. (Minn. Ct. App. opinion)
more: The Minnesota Supreme Court denied review on July 18, 2023. (Order reproduced in cert. petition appendix, No. 23-416)
The U.S. Supreme Court denied Chauvin's petition for certiorari on November 20, 2023. (U.S. Supreme Court docket No. 23-416)

entries.headline: 1.7 Derek Chauvin: federal civil rights case

lines: A federal grand jury indicted Chauvin, Thao, Kueng and Lane on May 6, 2021. (Thao verdict)

In his federal plea agreement, Chauvin admitted that he "willfully deprived George Perry Floyd, Jr., of his constitutional rights" and that "[t]his offense resulted in bodily injury to, and the death of George Floyd." (Plea agreement, D. Minn. 0:21-cr-00108, Doc. 142)

He also admitted "that his willful use of unreasonable force resulted in Mr. Floyd's bodily injury and death because his actions impaired Mr. Floyd's ability to obtain and maintain sufficient oxygen to sustain Mr. Floyd's life." (Plea agreement, Doc. 142)
The plea also covered a separate 18 U.S.C. § 242 count for force used on a juvenile on September 4, 2017. (Amended judgment, Doc. 529)

On July 7, 2022, the court imposed 240 months and 12 months, consecutive (252 months). The judgment adjusted this to 245 months for prior state custody, to run concurrently with the state sentence. (Amended judgment, Doc. 529)
A federal jury convicted Tou Thao, J. Alexander Kueng and Thomas Lane on all charges after a trial from January 24 to February 21, 2022. (Thao verdict)
more: In state court, Lane pleaded guilty to "aiding manslaughter in the second degree," with a recommended executed term of 36 months. (Lane guilty-plea filing; MN Attorney General, May 18, 2022)
Kueng's state plea petition covers Count 2, second-degree manslaughter, with an executed prison term of 42 months. (Kueng plea petition; MN Attorney General, Oct. 24, 2022)
After a stipulated-evidence bench trial, Judge Cahill found Thao "GUILTY of the offense of aiding and abetting second-degree manslaughter." (Thao verdict; MN Attorney General, May 2, 2023)

sources.label: ACLED, "Demonstrations and Political Violence in America: New Data for Summer 2020"

lines: ACLED, the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, is a research organization. It reported that "[i]n more than 93% of all demonstrations connected to the movement, demonstrators have not engaged in violence or destructive activity." (ACLED, "Demonstrations and Political Violence in America: New Data for Summer 2020")
ACLED counted more than 7,750 BLM-linked demonstrations in more than 2,440 locations between May 26 and August 22, 2020. (ACLED)
ACLED reported that violent demonstrations took place in fewer than 220 locations. (ACLED)
ACLED notes three limits on these figures. (ACLED)
more: Its violent category "includes events where violence may have been initially instigated by police or other actors."
The data counts events, not how large or destructive each event was.
The period ends August 22, 2020, before the Kenosha unrest.

entries.headline: R2020-01 · CNN (Early Start with Christine Romans and Laura Jarrett)

lines: What was said: On-screen caption "FIERY BUT MOSTLY PEACEFUL PROTESTS AFTER POLICE SHOOTING" shown over burning vehicles and buildings in Kenosha, WI.
Said by CNN (Early Start with Christine Romans and Laura Jarrett)
Began: Aug 25, 2020 (CNN Early Start, ~5:05 AM ET / 3:05 AM MDT) | Ended: single broadcast segment Original transcript/video

What the record shows: The caption ran over live footage of structures on fire. In the same segment, correspondent Omar Jimenez said 'what you're seeing is one of multiple locations that have been burning in Kenosha' and contrasted the night with daytime demonstrations he called 'largely peaceful.' Anchor Christine Romans said 'At least three buildings were on fire in Kenosha overnight.' The caption described the scene on screen as mostly peaceful while it showed arson. The reporter's spoken words did separate day from night. It aired Aug 25, not Aug 24. ACLED's nationwide 'mostly peaceful' aggregate ends Aug 22 and does not cover Kenosha.
record.label: Rated misleading

lines: What was said: Seattle's Capitol Hill protest zone was "more like a block party atmosphere. It's not an armed takeover"; "there is no threat right now to the public"; "We could have the Summer of Love."
Said by Seattle Mayor Jenny Durkan
Began: Jun 11, 2020 (CNN Cuomo Prime Time) | Ended: Jul 1, 2020 (zone cleared under Mayor's emergency order) Original transcript/video

What the record shows: The quotes are exact from CNN's transcript. Durkan's own Executive Order 2020-08 (June 30) later recorded several things: 'A pervasive presence of firearms and other weapons has been well-documented'; a 525% increase in person-related crime in the area June 2-30 vs. 2019; homicides on June 20 and June 29; and first responders 'denied safe access... by hostile crowds, including armed individuals.'

Context Timing caveat: the remarks were made June 11, before both homicides. 'Summer of Love' answered a question about how long the zone would last and was partly speculative. The EO's crime window (June 2-30) overlaps the interview date. The EO itself also says 'much of the expression has been peaceful.' The rating applies only to the "no threat... to the public" and "not an armed takeover" remarks, not to the "Summer of Love" phrase.
record.label: Rated misleading

entries.headline: 5.1 Minneapolis and the State of Minnesota

sources.label: Hillard Heintze, "An After-Action Review of City Agencies' Responses to Activities Directly Following George Floyd's Death on May 25, 2020"

lines: The City of Minneapolis commissioned an independent after-action review from Hillard Heintze. The report was issued March 7, 2022 and covers May 25–June 3, 2020. (Hillard Heintze, "An After-Action Review of City Agencies' Responses to Activities Directly Following George Floyd's Death on May 25, 2020")
The review found that "the City of Minneapolis did not use its emergency operations plan effectively to guide its response." (After-Action Review)
The review states that on May 28, 2020, "the MPD chief announced the decision to abandon the 3rd Precinct. At 10:15 p.m., MPD leadership ordered the 3rd Precinct evacuated." (After-Action Review)
It continues: "Once the MPD abandoned the 3rd Precinct, rioters assumed control of the building and quickly set fires within and to additional buildings in the area." (After-Action Review)
more: The Minnesota Senate report's MPD timeline lists "2155 hours – Order given to Evacuate the 3rd precinct" and "2215 hours – PRECINCT 3 IS COMPROMISED." (MN Senate report)
The two documents give different times for the evacuation order: 9:55 p.m. in the Senate report and 10:15 p.m. in the city's review. (MN Senate report; After-Action Review)

National Guard, the city review's account: The city review found that the Mayor made a verbal request to the Governor on the evening of May 27, followed by a written request. It found that "the detailed information critical to the mission, required by MNG for approval as detailed in the policy, was not included in any of the initial requests." (After-Action Review)
The same review found that "subsequent requests on May 28 included the required information and fulfilled the MNG requirements for activation." (After-Action Review)

National Guard, the Senate majority's account: The Senate report stated that "Governor Walz first mobilized the Minnesota National Guard on the afternoon of Thursday, May 28, 18 hours after Mayor Frey requested assistance." It added that the Guard "was not fully mobilized until four days after the first building was burned." (MN Senate report)
Governor Walz's Executive Order 20-64, signed May 28, 2020, declared a peacetime emergency and directed that the Adjutant General order the Guard to state active duty. (EO 20-64)
EO 20-64 stated that "some individuals have engaged in unlawful and dangerous activity, including arson, rioting, looting." (EO 20-64)
It also stated that "the Mayors of both cities have requested the assistance of the Minnesota National Guard." (EO 20-64)
Executive Order 20-65 imposed a curfew in Minneapolis and Saint Paul from 8:00 p.m. Friday, May 29 to 6:00 a.m. Saturday, May 30, and again the following night. (EO 20-65)

sources.label: City of Portland, Mayor Wheeler directive, Sept. 10, 2020
Opinion and Order, Rosenblum v. John Does 1-10, D. Or. 3:20-cv-01161, Doc. 23

lines: In 2020, the Oregon Legislature passed HB 4208, which bars law enforcement from using tear gas for crowd control "except in circumstances constituting a riot." (Enrolled HB 4208, 2020 First Special Session)
HB 4208 also requires two announcements and time to evacuate before tear gas is used. (Enrolled HB 4208)

On September 10, 2020, Mayor Ted Wheeler, acting as police commissioner, stated: "effective immediately and until further notice, I am directing the Portland Police to end the use of CS gas for crowd control." (City of Portland, Mayor Wheeler directive, Sept. 10, 2020)
In the same statement Wheeler said: "During the last hundred days Portland, Multnomah County and State Police have all relied on CS gas where there is a threat to life safety." (City of Portland)
more: He also said: "Arson, vandalism, and violence are not going to drive change in this community." (City of Portland)

Federal-state dispute: Oregon's Attorney General sued federal agencies on July 17, 2020, seeking to stop federal officers from seizing protesters in Portland. On July 24, 2020, U.S. District Judge Michael Mosman denied a temporary restraining order, finding "the State of Oregon lacks standing." (Opinion and Order, Rosenblum v. John Does 1-10, D. Or. 3:20-cv-01161, Doc. 23)
Judge Mosman ruled "without reaching the merits of the underlying claims." (Opinion and Order, Doc. 23)
Oregon later dismissed the case without prejudice, "[i]n light of the defendant agencies having evidently ceased the conduct at issue." (Notice of voluntary dismissal, Doc. 28)

lines: The Seattle Office of Inspector General's city-commissioned Sentinel Event Review reports: "On the evening of June 8th, SPD evacuated its East Precinct." (Seattle OIG Sentinel Event Review, Wave 3)
The review states: "For more than a year after the evacuation, it was unclear who authorized SPD to vacate the precinct and why." (Seattle OIG SER Wave 3)
The review states: "The CHOP existed until July 1, 2020." (Seattle OIG SER Wave 3)

On June 20, 2020, the Seattle Police Department reported that a 19-year-old man was killed in a shooting inside the protest area. It said officers were "met by a violent crowd that prevented officers safe access to the victims." (SPD Blotter, June 20, 2020)
more: On June 29, 2020, SPD reported that a 16-year-old was killed and a 14-year-old injured in a shooting on 12th Avenue. It said that "the crime scene had been disturbed." (SPD Blotter, June 29, 2020)

Mayor Durkan's Executive Order 2020-08 states that after the June 20 shooting, first responders "were denied safe access to the area by hostile crowds, including armed individuals." (Seattle EO 2020-08)

The order states that on June 29, "a juvenile was shot and killed," and that "[e]vidence indicates that this murder may have been committed by individual(s) 'occupying' the area." (Seattle EO 2020-08)

The order records "[a]n increase of 525%, 22 additional incidents, in person-related crime … between June 2nd and June 30th, 2020, compared to the same period of time in 2019." That increase included two additional homicides, six additional robberies and sixteen additional aggravated assaults. (Seattle EO 2020-08)
The order states: "A pervasive presence of firearms and other weapons has been well-documented." (Seattle EO 2020-08)
SPD announced on July 1, 2020 that the Mayor had issued an emergency order regarding the protest zone. (SPD Blotter, July 1, 2020)

The Sentinel Event Review reports that the Office of Police Accountability found that "an SPD Captain appointed an officer to make false radio broadcasts to draw protestors away from the CHOP." The false broadcasts, on June 8, 2020, reported Proud Boys moving toward the zone, and OPA found they violated SPD policy. (Seattle OIG SER Wave 3)

The review also reports that "No police reports were filed related to extortion of businesses within or around the CHOP." This came after SPD said at a June 10 press conference that it had "heard anecdotally reports" of extortion. (Seattle OIG SER Wave 3)

The Seattle City Council passed an ordinance banning police use of crowd-control weapons. On July 24, 2020, at the U.S. government's request, U.S. District Judge James Robart granted the government's motion for a temporary restraining order. The order enjoined the ordinance's "implementation date" until the city followed the procedures in its federal consent decree, and the court stated that it "does not enjoin the CCW Ordinance itself." (TRO, United States v. City of Seattle, W.D. Wash. 2:12-cv-01282)

NAME, A Guide for Manner of Death Classification (1st ed., Feb. 2002; Hanzlick, Hunsaker, Davis):

"Homicide occurs when death results from a volitional act committed by another person to cause fear, harm, or death. Intent to cause death is a common element but is not required … the classification of Homicide for the purposes of death certification is a 'neutral' term and neither indicates nor implies criminal intent, which remains a determination within the province of legal processes."
"the manner of death is unnatural when injury hastened the death of one already vulnerable to significant or even life-threatening disease."

"Deaths due to positional restraint induced by law enforcement personnel or to choke holds or other measures to subdue may be classified as Homicide. In such cases, there may not be intent to kill, but the death results from one or more intentional, volitional, potentially harmful acts directed at the decedent."
more: The same passage adds that the classification has "some value … toward reducing the public perception that a 'cover up' is being perpetrated."

"Seldom, for the purpose of manner-of-death classification, is 'beyond a reasonable doubt' required." Death-certificate findings "only represent the certifier's opinion and are not written in stone or legally binding."
Hennepin County ME press release (June 1, 2020): "Manner of death is not a legal determination of culpability or intent."
New York AG Prude report (2021), same principle: the ME's homicide designation "is not a legal culpability determination"; it means the death occurred "at the hands of another."
CDC/NCHS Medical Examiners' and Coroners' Handbook on Death Registration (2003): the file could not be retrieved. It is not quoted here.
Minnesota causation law (quoted in the Oct. 21, 2020 probable-cause order):
A defendant's act is a substantial causal factor if it "contributed to the death" (State v. Torkelson, 404 N.W.2d 352, 357 (Minn. App. 1987)).
The State need not prove "the specific mechanism of death," and the act need not be "the sole cause of death" (State v. Gatson, 801 N.W.2d 134, 148 (Minn. 2011)).

State v. Smith, 119 N.W.2d 838, 848 (Minn. 1962): "It is immaterial that defendant did not know that the deceased was suffering from a condition which facilitated the killing … Responsibility attaches for an injury which causes or contributes to death although the condition from which the victim was suffering might itself have caused death in time."
State v. King, 367 N.W.2d 599, 602 (Minn. App. 1985): the victim's physical condition "will not excuse or minimize its consequences."
State v. James, 144 N.W. 216 (Minn. 1913): pneumonia after a stabbing.
A superseding cause must be "the sole cause" (Gatson; State v. Jaworsky, 505 N.W.2d 638).
The court concluded: "In short, Floyd's pre-existing medical conditions cannot defeat causation."
